SEC15A-01.note: 'that' takes its number from 'components' in 'one of the few components that', so plural 'are'; present tense matches 'is' and 'may spend'. A is very attractive because the sentence's subject (balance spring) and 'one' are singular; informal 'one of the few that is' is not accepted in edited prose. C/D fail on tense.

SEC15A-02.note: 'for many generations by the time ... arrived ... in 1896' requires past perfect progressive. B (simple past progressive) is the strongest distractor; A and C clash with the past reference point, but you have to read to 'by the time' to see that.

SEC15A-03.note: Head noun is singular 'core'; 'together with dozens of samples' is a parenthetical modifier, not a compound subject, so 'indicates'. B tempts through the apparent compound and the nearby plural 'huts'; C/D passive cannot take the 'that' clause with this subject.

SEC15A-04.note: The subject is the infinitive phrase 'To reconstruct ... priests', which is singular, so 'requires'. C is attractive after the plural list 'farmers, innkeepers, and village priests'; A and B leave the sentence with no finite verb, which a test-taker who spots the missing verb rejects at once.

SEC15A-05.note: The walls are the tunnel's (singular), so possessive 'its'. C and D are contractions that can never precede a noun here, so only A versus B is live; A tempts via plural 'slopes'/'seeds' nearby.
SEC15A-05.drop_reason: Too easy for the module-2 hard route: two options are contractions that can be rejected without reading the sentence, leaving their/its, which most test-takers get right. The key is correct; it is held only on difficulty.

SEC15A-06.note: 'both recorded ... and copied' is a correlative compound predicate; no punctuation separates its halves, and C/D break the 'both...and' pair (and D leaves a subjectless fragment). B is attractive because the first element is long and contains a list; 'copied' with no subject shows the compound predicate only if one remembers 'both'.

SEC15A-07.note: 'an island whose ...' is a nonrestrictive appositive renaming Murano, set off with a comma. D makes a fragment (no main verb in 'An island whose ...'), B puts a semicolon before a non-clause; A, with no punctuation, reads as garbled to most test-takers.

SEC15B-01.note: Head noun 'escapements' is plural, and 'since ... 1774' requires present perfect: 'have kept'. C is strongest, because the singular nouns 'prototype' and 'its drawings' sit closest to the verb; A/B fail on tense, but 'since' lies beyond the four-word window.

SEC15B-02.note: The rags are acted on ('by itinerant peddlers') in the 1340s, so past passive 'were collected'. C reads as active past (the rags did the collecting) and is the strongest lure; B and D fail on tense and voice.

SEC15B-03.note: 'in the spring of 1857' fixes simple past. B (present perfect with a specific past date) is the only semi-plausible lure; A and D are plainly wrong once the date is seen. Too easy for the hard route.
SEC15B-03.drop_reason: Too easy for the hard route: the date '1857' fixes simple past, and the only plausible lure is the present perfect. The key is correct; it is held only on difficulty.

SEC15B-04.note: Singular head 'silkworm' separated by a long appositive that ends in plural 'farmers tending mulberry groves', so 'depends'. A is the lure; B and C leave the sentence without a main verb.

SEC15B-05.note: 'puzzled over how ... possessed' is an indirect question inside a declarative sentence, so it ends with a period; a new independent clause follows. A (question mark) is the strong lure; C is a comma splice; D runs on and reads as garbled.

SEC15B-06.note: 'its bronze ... proving too brittle' is an absolute phrase (participle, no finite verb), attached with a comma. B and C look right until 'proving', which shows no independent clause follows; D jams two nouns together. A dash would also work but is not offered.

SEC15B-07.note: 'drawing water from a single spring above the harbor' is a restrictive modifier identifying which households, so no punctuation; every other option puts a single mark between subject and verb 'escaped'. A tempts as a half-built nonessential pair.

tells: The semicolon option is never the key in any punctuation item (A-06, A-07, B-06; B-05 has none). Period+capital is the key only in B-05, the one item whose option set is ?/./,/none.

A-06, A-07 and B-06 share one option frame (none / comma / semicolon / period); the key is the comma twice and none once, so 'pick the comma' wins 2 of 3. Adding B-07 (comma, dash, none, colon; key none), the plainest option wins 2 of 4.

Subject-verb items (A-03, A-04, B-04): the singular -s form is the key every time the head noun is buried behind plurals. A-01 and B-01 break this, so it is not a clean tell, but A-04 and B-04 together teach 'long modifier full of plurals -> pick singular'.
Verb-form items with two nonfinite options (A-04: requiring/to require; B-04: depending/to depend) let a test-taker strike two options without parsing; those items are effectively two-way.
Key letter spread is balanced (A4 B3 C3 D4); no positional tell.
near_duplicates: singular head behind a long modifier ending in plural nouns; options plural / -ing / to- / -s; key -s
long subject with a second noun group attached by 'together with' / 'and in'; agreement with the head noun, singular vs plural x tense/voice grid
noun + following noun phrase that is not a clause (appositive / absolute); none/comma/semicolon/period; key comma
tense fixed by an explicit past date (1340s / 1857), lures in present and perfect

phase2_note: All 14 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses). Every explanation's reasoning reaches the key and rejects each distractor on a correct rule. I found no exclusivity or key disputes. A-05 and B-03 are recommended for drop on difficulty alone (easy, weak distractors, wrong band for the hard route), not on correctness. Phase-1 cross-item tells still apply: the semicolon is never the key, the comma wins 2 of the 3 none/comma/semicolon/period sets, and A-04/B-04 each have two nonfinite options a test-taker can strike without parsing.
